title: JPMorgan Stock Slides on Epstein Probe Fears: Bitcoin Has No CEO to Drag Into the Scandal - CryptoPotato
content: Alongside the rest of the market, shares of JPMorgan Chase tanked at the end of the previous week, but there’s more to the story. JPM’s decline also came after reports emerged that Senate Democrats are preparing a fresh investigation into the banking behemoth’s relationship with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Although there’s no real connection with Bitcoin, we decided to still cover this and highlight the awkwardness, as JPM’s CEO, Jamie Dimon, has spent years bashing the crypto industry. CNBC reported after the Blue-nami in the US midterms that Democratic staff on the Senate Finance Committee plan to examine how senior JPM executives handled Epstein as they take control of Congress early next year. Mary Erdoes, CEO of the bank’s Asset & Wealth Management Division, is expected to be among the high-profile names in the investigations. “The US government had damning information ​about Epstein’s crimes that it failed to share ​with us or other banks. We regret any association we had with ‌him, ⁠but we did not help him commit his crimes,” commented a spokesperson from the bank. The market reaction was immediate as JPM shares tanked by over 4% to under $340 on Thursday. The sell-off essentially erased the stock’s post-midterm rally. Although the bank continues to deny any wrongdoing, it previously agreed to pay $365 million in settlements related to Epstein. We admit there’s no official confirmation that JPM has done anything wrong, and we don’t expect it to come to light if it did, because it’s one of the world’s largest banks. And we know how banks are treated in almost any situation (recall the 2008 banking crisis and the subsequent lack of any real consequences). Nevertheless, the irony is still worth pointing out. JPM’s long-serving CEO, Jamie Dimon, has been bashing BTC for years. He has called it a “fraud,” “worthless,” a “pet rock,” and a “decentralized Ponzi scheme.” All bad and, in some cases, illegal names. He also advised investors to stay away from crypto and told lawmakers that if he were running the US government, he would “close it down.” The hypocrisy is glaring when we look at what the bank has done lately. It now lets institutional clients use BTC and ETH as collateral; it supports crypto-related services; it participated in BlackRock’s spot Bitcoin ETF infrastructure; and it recently projected that bitcoin could outperform US large-cap stocks and gold over the next 10-15 years. But there’s another contrast. Bitcoin has no CEO, board of directors, wealth-management division, or customer relationship with Jeffrey Epstein – or anyone else, for that matter. The protocol itself cannot make a questionable client decision, hide internal correspondence, or become subject to congressional scrutiny over corporate conduct. People or companies using BTC can still appear in investigations and criminal records, but reputational and governance risks belong to institutions and individuals, not the decentralized Bitcoin network itself. title: JP Morgan Athlete Center of Excellence: athletes need a financial playbook now more than ever - Fortune
content:
Adam Frank is head of wealth planning and advice at J.P. Morgan Wealth Management. He and his team are responsible for wealth planning, thought leadership and strategic planning for individual clients, and he oversees the firm’s Athlete Center of Excellence. J.P. Morgan’s Athlete Center of Excellence and the JPMorganChase Athlete Council are both named in this piece. For years, the playbook was simple: athletes focused on their sport first, and financial planning came later. Only after signing a professional contract did they typically hire advisors, accountants and attorneys — and start thinking seriously about managing their wealth. That timeline often no longer reflects reality. The sports industry has made tremendous strides in creating new ways for athletes to earn money. The next challenge is ensuring they have the knowledge and support to manage it. Today, many athletes start earning meaningful income long before they turn professional. The College Sports Commission estimates that student-athletes received $1.77 billion in revenue-sharing pay in 2025-2026. Name, Image and Likeness (NIL) opportunities have accelerated that shift, giving student-athletes access to sponsorships and business opportunities while they’re still in school. At the same time, the demand for financial guidance is growing. The 2022 NCAA Student-Athlete Well-Being Study found that many have a strong desire for more resources on financial literacy and taxes. There is a big focus on creating more earning opportunities for athletes. We now need to put the same energy into helping athletes prepare for the financial responsibilities that come with them. Too often, financial education starts after the money arrives. By then, habits have already formed and important decisions may have already been made. The reality is that some of the most important financial choices for athletes happen before they sign a major contract. How do taxes work? How much should I save? How do I navigate money conversations with friends and family? Who should I trust? These aren’t professional athlete questions. They’re life questions. And athletes are encountering them earlier than ever before. One thing I’ve learned from conversations with athletes in my role at J.P. Morgan’s Athlete Center of Excellence is that they’re eager for this guidance. I’ve spoken with current players who — when they were earning NIL income — budgeted for spending and invested the rest, only to find themselves short on cash when tax payments were due. They had the right pieces in place but only became fully engaged when there was a need to be. I’ve seen a lot of players learn to bring in their financial advisor this way — relying on the advisor to then quarterback communication among their agent, attorney and accountant. Athletes should not be expected to be financial experts. Just as athletes rely on coaches, trainers, nutritionists and medical professionals, they should be able to rely on trusted specialists for financial guidance. But athletes should also have basic financial knowledge so they can ask thoughtful questions, evaluate advice and make informed decisions. I often encourage athletes to think of themselves as the CEO of their own business. You don’t have to master every function of the organization, but you should understand how the pieces fit together and remain engaged in the decisions that affect your future. That mindset has become increasingly important as athletes build personal brands and create new income streams earlier in their careers. Today’s athletes aren’t just managing contracts. Many are navigating partnerships, content opportunities, business ventures and NIL deals at a young age. The financial complexity has increased, and adequate preparation needs to increase with it. The answer isn’t limiting opportunity for athletes. It’s building a stronger foundation of education and support around it. First, we need to start earlier. Financial fundamentals should be introduced in high school, before athletes encounter significant earnings. By the time money arrives, the framework for managing it should already be in place. Second, financial education cannot be a one-time conversation. Athletes’ needs evolve as they move from high school to college, turn professional and transition out of sports. The guidance they receive should evolve alongside them. One of the reasons the JPMorganChase Athlete Council was created was to hear directly from athletes. This way, we can better understand the financial questions they’re facing and develop resources that reflect their real-world experiences, not our assumptions. Athletic careers are unlike almost any other profession. Most people earn income over several decades. Athletes often earn a huge portion of their career income over a much shorter period of time. Opportunities can arrive unexpectedly, and they can disappear just as quickly. If we want athletes to thrive not only during their playing careers but throughout the rest of their lives, we need to start with financial education long before the first major paycheck arrives. Coherent’s Datacenter and Communications segment generated approximately $1.95 billion in quarterly revenue, up 79% year over year, demonstrating the impact of expanding AI infrastructure demand. Dimon argued a core strength of the dollar is its ability to be spent freely without any capital restrictions imposed by the U.S. government, compared to other nations. title: DTE Energy To Sell DTE Vantage Business For $3 Billion To J.P. Morgan Asset Management Investors And Expand Utility Investments To $44 Billion - Pulse 2.0
content: DTE Energy, a Detroit-based electric and natural gas utility company, has entered into an agreement to sell all of its non-utility DTE Vantage business substantially for approximately $3 billion to institutional investors advised by the Global Infrastructure group at J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The transaction will support DTE’s strategy of concentrating on regulated utility operations and expanding infrastructure investments across Michigan. The sale is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions. The transaction includes substantially all DTE Vantage assets, excluding EES Coke. DTE plans to direct additional resources toward its electric and natural gas utilities, which serve approximately 2.3 million electric customers in Southeast Michigan and 1.4 million natural gas customers statewide. The company outlined approximately $44 billion in customer-focused capital investments planned over the next five years, including projects involving grid modernization, reliability improvements, cleaner electricity generation, and infrastructure supporting growing energy demand. Through the first nine months of 2026, DTE invested nearly $4.1 billion in its regulated utilities and remains on track to invest approximately $6.1 billion during the full year. The planned divestiture also comes as DTE expands its infrastructure to accommodate demand from hyperscale data centers. Following approval from the Michigan Public Service Commission, DTE is moving forward with energy supply agreements supporting two hyperscale data center customers in Michigan, including Google’s planned facility in Van Buren Township. DTE expects the agreements to generate substantial financial benefits for existing utility customers through 2045. Under the contracts, data center operators will cover the full cost of the electricity supply and grid investments required to serve their facilities. The company also expects the data centers to contribute billions of dollars to the electric system, helping reduce the share of system costs paid by existing customers. The agreements are intended to support economic development while protecting current ratepayers from infrastructure expenses associated with large new electricity consumers. DTE has also filed a 20-year Integrated Resource Plan with the Michigan Public Service Commission outlining its proposed approach to future electricity generation. The plan combines renewable energy, battery storage, nuclear power, and natural gas generation to meet changing electricity demand while maintaining reliability and managing customer costs. DTE remains committed to ending coal-fired electricity generation by 2032. Its latest resource plan targets an 84% reduction in carbon dioxide emissions and is projected to cost approximately $3.5 billion less than the company’s previous plan. The utility also completed the 100-megawatt Cold Creek Solar Park near Coldwater, Michigan, through its renewable energy partnership with Ford Motor Company. The project supports Ford’s objective of assembling every vehicle manufactured in Michigan using the equivalent of 100% carbon-free electricity by the end of 2027. At the end of 2025, DTE operated 20 wind parks and 34 solar parks, collectively generating enough electricity to power more than 900,000 homes. The company also reported providing customers with access to nearly $125 million in energy assistance during 2025. Alongside the DTE Vantage sale announcement, DTE reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $470 million, or $2.25 per diluted share, compared with $419 million, or $2.01 per share, during the prior-year quarter. Operating earnings increased to $481 million, or $2.30 per share, from $468 million, or $2.25 per share, in the third quarter of 2025. For the first nine months of 2026, DTE reported net income of $999 million, compared with $1.09 billion during the corresponding period in 2025. The company confirmed its full-year 2026 operating earnings guidance of $7.59 to $7.73 per share and provided a 2027 pro forma operating earnings baseline within the same range, reflecting the proposed DTE Vantage divestiture. Lazard is serving as exclusive financial advisor to DTE Energy on the sale, while Kirkland & Ellis is providing legal counsel. The transaction represents a significant portfolio restructuring for DTE, allowing the company to narrow its focus on regulated utility services while advancing an expanded investment program designed to support Michigan’s long-term electricity and natural gas requirements. “DTE Vantage has been a strong non-utility business and valued part of DTE Energy for more than 30 years. This transaction advances our strategy to focus our resources on our regulated electric and gas utilities, where we see significant opportunities to invest on behalf of customers and communities. The sale supports our plan to deliver meaningful affordability benefits for customers, strengthens our ability to execute a substantial utility investment plan and positions DTE as a high-growth, premium utility with a stronger long-term outlook.” “Strong financial performance through the third quarter of 2026 positions us to continue investing in Michigan’s energy infrastructure while delivering long-term value for our customers, communities and shareholders.” Thank you for visiting Pulse 2.0. title: Double-digit price declines in property cat reinsurance likely to persist, says JP Morgan - Reinsurance News
content:
JP Morgan, the US-based global investment bank and financial services company, expects double-digit price declines in property catastrophe reinsurance to persist into 2027, as strong industry profitability, relatively low natural catastrophe losses and an influx of capital continue to put pressure on rates. The reinsurance market, and notably property and property cat lines, have been experiencing softer pricing conditions for some time, but 2026 marked an acceleration in the pace of reductions. Following a period of exceptionally high rates in 2023 and 2024 after the so-called reset, pricing has moved progressively lower, with more substantial decreases recorded across the latest renewal periods. JP Morgan cited figures from reinsurance broker Marsh Re, formerly known as Guy Carpenter, showing that average reinsurance prices declined by approximately 12% at the January 2026 renewals. The downward trend continued into the mid-year renewal period, with global property catastrophe rates falling by 16% at the July 2026 renewals. The investment bank anticipates additional pricing pressure at the January 2027 renewals, particularly within property catastrophe lines, where it expects double-digit decreases to continue. JP Morgan attributed this outlook to several factors, including the sector’s sustained strong returns on equity (ROE), relatively benign catastrophe experience during 2026 to date and the availability of new sources of capital. JP Morgan noted that reinsurers have recorded particularly favourable financial results since 2023, with average ROEs remaining in the high teens. The bank compared this performance with the period following Hurricane Katrina, when increased property catastrophe rates and elevated interest rates supported similarly strong industry returns. However, the investment bank cautioned that extended periods of consistently high profitability have been relatively uncommon in the reinsurance industry. Historically, fluctuations in catastrophe losses have contributed to greater volatility in earnings than has been observed in recent years, suggesting that the current level of profitability may become harder to sustain. JP Morgan also indicated that the financial consequences of declining reinsurance rates are beginning to emerge, particularly in underwriting performance, despite the sector’s continued resilience in the near term. The bank pointed to Munich Re as one of the first major reinsurers to demonstrate the effects of weaker pricing on its combined ratio expectations during 2026. At the beginning of the year, Munich Re’s normalised combined ratio was expected to stand at 80%, but this had deteriorated to approximately 82% by the second quarter. While other reinsurers have so far experienced a more limited impact, JP Morgan believes the broader industry will find it increasingly difficult to offset continued rate reductions. The bank therefore expects underwriting margins to face growing pressure over the next two years as lower pricing gradually affects financial performance. title: JP Morgan’s Justin Nelson weighs the cost of a foundation - Cyprus Mail
content:
Deciding to give is the easy part for most wealthy families. The harder call comes next: where should the money sit before it reaches a charity? Justin Nelson hears that question often. A managing director at J.P. Morgan Private Bank, he heads the Asset Management and Financial Principals Coverage Team in Connecticut, a 20-person group that advises leaders in hedge funds, private equity and real estate. Justin Nelson’s JP Morgan profile notes that he also manages relationships with endowments and foundations across New York and Connecticut. For many of his clients, the choice comes down to two structures: a private foundation or a donor-advised fund, known as a DAF. “I sometimes describe a donor-advised fund as giving you much of the experience of having a charitable foundation without having to operate a foundation,” Nelson says. A foundation offers the most control. A family can seat its own board, bring children and grandchildren into grant decisions and put its name on an institution meant to outlast its founders. Nelson says that appeal is real for families who want philanthropy itself to become a family enterprise. Then comes the overhead. JP Morgan’s own side-by-side comparison of the two vehicles lays out the rules. A private foundation must distribute 5% of the fair market value of its assets each year, and any shortfall left undistributed past the deadline is hit with a 30% excise tax. Grants are disclosed publicly through an annual Form 990-PF filing. Initial funding typically starts between $1 million and $2 million, before legal and accounting fees are paid. The IRS also levies a 1.39% excise tax on a foundation’s net investment income. The deduction isn’t as generous, either. Cash gifts to a foundation can be deducted up to 30% of adjusted gross income, compared with 60% for a DAF. For publicly traded stock and other appreciated assets, the ceiling drops to 20%, against 30% for a DAF. None of that runs itself. Nelson says a foundation’s control comes bundled with administrative, tax, reporting and governance work, and someone in the family has to own it. “A foundation makes sense when the infrastructure itself is part of what you want to build. A donor-advised fund makes sense when you primarily want an efficient vehicle for giving.” A DAF works more like a charitable account. The donor contributes assets, takes the deduction when eligible, then recommends grants over months or years. The paperwork is handled by the sponsoring organization. JP Morgan’s comparison puts the typical minimum contribution at around $10,000, with no startup costs and no annual payout requirement. That low barrier shows up in the data. DAFs held about $326 billion in assets in 2024, up from $250 billion a year earlier, according to the first Annual DAF Report from the DAF Research Collaborative, which was compiled from IRS filings and reported by The Chronicle of Philanthropy. Donors put $89.6 billion into the accounts that year and granted $64.9 billion to charities. Private foundations still gave more: $118.5 billion. Nelson’s explanation is short: simplicity. A DAF separates the timing of the tax decision from the timing of the charitable one, so someone who sells a business, exercises stock options or books a large capital gain can make a bigger contribution that year and pick the recipients later. “A donor-advised fund lets you make the financial decision today and the philanthropic decisions over time,” he says. Washington gave that feature new weight. Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, itemizers can deduct charitable gifts only above a floor of 0.5% of adjusted gross income starting in 2026, and top-bracket taxpayers get a deduction worth 35% instead of 37%, Thomson Reuters reported. Plenty of donors didn’t wait. National Philanthropic Trust, one of the country’s largest DAF sponsors, opened more than 3,700 new accounts in the final two months of 2025, up from nearly 1,700 in the same stretch of 2024, The Philadelphia Inquirer reported. Its 2025 grants climbed 72% to a little over $10 billion. Picking a vehicle is half the work. “The most tax-efficient charitable gift is often not a check,” Nelson says. Highly appreciated securities are the classic case. Donated directly, they can support a charity while avoiding the capital gains tax a sale would have triggered. High-income years, liquidity events and portfolio transitions can all open a window to give more, and Nelson says a DAF helps because a family can make a large contribution when the deduction is worth the most without sending every dollar out the door at once. The estate plan belongs in that conversation. For families that already intend to leave assets to charity, coordinating those bequests with what heirs receive can make the whole plan more efficient. “You don’t want the investment strategy, the tax strategy, the estate plan and the charitable plan operating independently. The real opportunity comes when you design them together,” he says. Nelson, who has served on the board of the Breast Cancer Alliance, has seen giving from the other side of the table. His advice for families that haven’t started skips the structure chart. One approach he suggests: agree on a few shared causes that take 60% or 70% of the annual giving budget, and let individual family members direct the rest. “Before asking, ‘Which charity should we give to?’ I think families should ask, ‘What problems do we care about solving?’” Nelson says. The right structure, he adds, depends on each family’s tax and estate circumstances. That’s a decision to make with tax and legal advisors in the room. title: JPM Flags Higher Rate Risks: Can Its Balance Sheet Stay Resilient? - TradingView
content: JPMorgan JPM remains focused on maintaining balance sheet resilience amid expectations of structurally higher interest rates. At the Nov. 5 BancAnalysts Association of Boston Conference, Charles Bristow, head of Treasury and chief investment officer, emphasized disciplined duration management, stable operating deposits and rigorous stress testing to navigate interest rate volatility. Bristow noted that JPMorgan has historically avoided excessive exposure to longer-duration securities, helping limit valuation risks as interest rates increased. Its emphasis on operating deposits linked to payments, custody and checking activities also supports funding stability, although unusually sharp rate increases could pressure deposit costs. The company's underlying performance reinforces this resilience. During the first nine months of 2026, reported net interest income (NII) increased 11% year over year to $77.9 billion. NII excluding Markets rose 4% to $71.7 billion, supported by deposit and loan growth. JPMorgan expects fourth-quarter 2026 NII of approximately $28 billion, implying full-year NII of $106.2 billion, while NII excluding Markets is projected to be $97.2 billion. Its preliminary 2027 outlook projects NII excluding Markets of nearly $107 billion, reflecting almost 10% growth backed by balance sheet expansion and higher rates. However, Bristow cautioned that proposed regulatory capital requirements could undermine returns from certain low-risk intermediation activities. Rapid interest rate repricing and tighter systemwide liquidity also pose risks. Overall, JPMorgan's diversified franchise, disciplined asset-liability management and stable deposit base support its earnings outlook. Nevertheless, regulatory uncertainty, funding costs and interest rate volatility warrant monitoring, suggesting a balanced investment approach. How are JPM’s Peers Expected to Fare in a Higher-Rate Regime? Two close peers of JPMorgan are Bank of America BAC and Citigroup C. Bank of America is well-positioned to benefit from higher interest rates, supported by its asset-sensitive balance sheet, fixed-rate asset repricing and loan growth. Bank of America expects 2026 NII to increase approximately 8% year over year. However, higher deposit costs could partly offset these benefits. Citigroup is positioned to benefit from higher interest rates, given its asset-sensitive balance sheet, loan growth and investment portfolio repricing. title: The blue wave is changing the AI trade - J.P. Morgan Private Bank
content:
We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. We work with a variety of clients to help them achieve their unique ambitions. Our world-class economists, strategists, and investment specialists share their timely ideas and perspectives. We have worked with clients for more than 200 years to help them achieve their unique ambitions. The U.S. economy and the stock market have proven resilient in 2026, even in the face of higher interest rates, geopolitical volatility and yet another energy shock. Whereas the U.S. consumer, aided by fiscal stimulus and tax cuts, is still spending, a growing driver of GDP growth remains the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out. In the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, the Democratic party gained control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, setting the stage for gridlock with a Republican president—especially when it comes to the continued development and adoption of AI across the country. Investors feared a federal moratorium that mirrors some of the state-led initiatives to curb the build-out, in response to affordability and zoning concerns. So, it’s only natural that the outcome of the elections initially sent stock market futures plunging nearly 2% before rebounding with significant volatility in technology companies even days after the result. Democratic gains increase the likelihood of tougher scrutiny around data center development, electricity affordability and who pays for new grid infrastructure. This can create near-term uncertainty for sectors that trade in line with AI developments like utilities—especially those with exposure to fast-growing markets like Texas and Georgia that offer affordable land, labor and both energy and water access. Even as investors reprice that risk, the structural backdrop remains in place. Hyperscaler investment is expected to continue. Electrification and the grid build-out are still pressing needs in order to support higher power demand and capital spending. Stopping the data center build-out is still a tall order. Initial efforts to curb the data center build-out began over the summer. Any new policies to slow or restrict new connections would build on a process that’s already underway. More notable policy changes could be around who bears the costs of additional grid connections, changes to tax exemptions, stricter financial commitments and emergency curtailment requirements, among others. While much of this uncertainty was priced in leading into the elections, the magnitude of the Democratic gains was not. And that’s changing the nature of the tech trade underneath the hood. In an environment where regulation could change even if the most AI-friendly states, companies with existing compute and data center projects—like the hyperscalers—have the edge. Plus, additional regulatory proposals target new developments, not existing ones, which could strengthen the position of companies with operational data centers, secured power and established customers. Combined with any potential moderation in AI growth and the ability to meet greater construction and permitting standards, the established lead that some of the biggest tech companies have is even more beneficial relative to the parts of the tech trade that rely on the incremental build-out. And that’s something investors are already pricing, sending the message that owning productive capacity today is different from depending on its construction tomorrow—even if that means factoring in potential regulatory risk. Before the policy details have even been settled, or formally proposed, investors have already repriced these possibilities. It’s most visible in parts of the “picks and shovels” AI infrastructure trade—the part of the market that rallied on the certainty of the build-out even as the return on investment faced remain in question. The 24-month forward price-to-earnings ratio of the MVIS US Listed Semiconductor Index has halved since June. After trading at a peak of 22.5 times forward earnings in June, the index currently trades at 11.4 times forward earnings. That’s at a valuation lower than when investors were digesting the beginning of the conflict in Iran, Liberation Day and the stock market lows of 2022. It reflects a market questioning the durability of the industry’s earnings and continued growth in capital expenditures. But that’s where the opportunity may lie. Yes, regulation is subject to change, but the scale of economic growth that has come from this sector alone may bear some impact on the level and willingness to limit continued development. The AI trade is far from over, but it is evolving. Financing, regulatory and power constraints can mean a bumpy road ahead, but unless end demand falters, the risk of an inventory overhang and earnings slowdown may already be baked into valuations. As the structural backdrop of the AI build-out remains in place, the key is to determine which companies have the lead in an undeniable technological evolution that can broaden out in the years to come.
